mots.sens: This word means 'earth' or 'land.' It evokes not only a geographical location but also the idea of possession and inheritance. In the context of Genesis 12:1, it represents the land promised by God to Abram, symbolizing a new beginning and a divine destiny. Spiritually, it reminds us that God has a specific plan for each of us, calling us to leave our comfort zones to enter into His promises.

This term refers to a 'family' or 'clan.' It is related to notions of connection, belonging, and identity. In this verse, God asks Abram to detach from his family, emphasizing the importance of faithfulness to the divine call, even at the expense of family ties. Theologically, it teaches us that our relationship with God must take precedence over all others, calling us to radical obedience.

This verb means 'to go' or 'to walk.' It implies movement, action, and a response to a call. In the context of this passage, it represents Abram's initiative to follow God's voice. Spiritually, it challenges us regarding our own willingness to respond to God's call, to move in faith, and to step into the unknown with confidence.

1.epoque: This passage is set in a patriarchal context, around 2000 B.C., at a time when tribal and familial relationships were fundamental to the identity and survival of peoples.
1.passage: Genesis 12:1 marks the beginning of Abram's story, who is called by God to leave his familiar surroundings for an uncertain yet promising future. This chapter introduces the theme of the covenant between God and Abram, which will be central throughout the rest of Scripture.
1.culture: In ancient culture, leaving one's country and family was a significant act, often associated with personal sacrifices and risks. This underscores the strength of the divine call and the importance of faith in Hebrew culture.
1.interpretation: This verse illustrates the principle of obedience to God's call, even when it involves sacrifices. It reminds us that faith often requires leaving behind what is familiar to embrace what God has in store for us.
1.commentaire: Abram's call teaches us that God may ask us to step away from our comfort to fulfill His plans. By responding to this call, we demonstrate faith and obedience, which can lead to unexpected blessings. Let us be attentive to God's voice in our lives and ready to walk into the unknown with confidence.

mots.sens: This word refers to a 'nation' or 'people.' In the biblical context, it refers to a group of people united by cultural, linguistic, or religious ties. The root of this word emphasizes the idea of community and collective identity. Theologically, it evokes God's plan to form a set-apart people dedicated to Him.

This term means 'to bless' and implies a divine action that confers prosperity, protection, and favor. The root of this word is associated with the idea of bending the knee, symbolizing humility before God. In this verse, the blessing is promised not only to Abraham but also to those who follow him, highlighting the impact of this blessing on future generations.

This word means 'name' and represents the identity and reputation of a person. In Hebrew culture, a name is often linked to an individual's character and destiny. Here, the fact that God promises to make Abraham's 'name' great underscores the importance of his role in the history of salvation and how he will be honored in the ages to come.

This term means 'blessing' and evokes a divine gift that brings joy and prosperity. It is often used to denote favor or grace granted by God. In this verse, the blessing promised to Abraham is both personal and collective, indicating that his life will be a source of blessing for others, reinforcing the idea of responsibility towards others.

2.epoque: This passage is set in an ancient context, around the 20th century B.C., at a time when nomadic tribes and alliances between peoples were common in the Middle East.
2.passage: In Genesis 12, God calls Abraham to leave his homeland to enter into a divine promise. This chapter marks the beginning of the story of Israel and the special relationship between God and His people.
2.culture: The culture of the time valued alliances and familial blessings, and a person's name was central to the transmission of heritage and identity.
2.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that God has a plan for Abraham that extends beyond his own life. The promise of a great nation and a universal blessing announces Israel's role in the plan of salvation for humanity.
2.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God has a project for each of us, and He calls us to be instruments of blessing for others. By accepting His call, we participate in His work and divine plan, becoming witnesses of His grace and faithfulness in the world.

mots.sens: This word means 'to bless' and comes from the root that evokes the idea of prosperity and divine favor. In the context of this verse, it highlights the importance of the divine blessing granted to those who support Abraham and his descendants. Spiritually, it reveals that God's blessing is conditional upon our attitude towards His servants.

This term means 'to curse' and implies a curse or divine disapproval. It is often associated with negative consequences for those who oppose God's will. In the context of this verse, it highlights the seriousness of opposing those whom God has chosen, underscoring the divine protection over Abraham and his lineage.

This word means 'family' or 'clan,' and it refers to extended groups of people sharing blood or alliance ties. In this verse, it emphasizes that Abraham's blessing extends beyond his own family, encompassing all nations. This foreshadows the universality of the message of salvation through Christ.

The name of Abraham, which means 'father of a multitude,' is central to this verse. It symbolizes God's plan to gather all nations under His blessing. This reveals the scope of the divine covenant that extends to all who believe, thus announcing the coming of the Messiah.

3.epoque: This verse is set in the patriarchal context of the Old Testament, around 2000 B.C., a time when God established covenants with central figures like Abraham.
3.passage: In Genesis 12, God calls Abraham to leave his homeland for a promised land, marking the beginning of a new era for his people. This verse is part of the divine promise that establishes Abraham as the father of a great nation.
3.culture: In Semitic culture, blessing and cursing are powerful concepts, often linked to prosperity or calamity. Supporting a spiritual leader was seen as an act of faith and loyalty.
3.interpretation: This verse illustrates the relationship between divine blessing and how we treat God's chosen ones. It reminds us that our actions towards others, especially those chosen by God, have profound spiritual consequences.
3.commentaire: As believers, we are called to bless those around us and support God's work in the world. This passage encourages us to recognize the value of each person and to act with love and respect, knowing that our attitude can influence not only our lives but also those of future generations.

mots.sens: The name 'Abram' means 'exalted father' or 'father of a multitude.' This name is significant as it foreshadows God's promise to make him the father of a great nation. The root of the word evokes a position of dignity and responsibility, highlighting Abram's role in God's divine plan of redemption. Spiritually, it reminds us that God calls each of us to a role in His work, regardless of our age or situation.

The verb 'yatza' means 'to go out' or 'to depart.' In this context, it implies the idea of leaving a familiar place to enter into a new divine calling. It also evokes the concept of separation from the past to embrace a promising future. Theologically, it teaches us that the path of faith often involves steps of departure and transition toward what God has prepared for us.

The word 'El' is a term for God, meaning 'the Almighty' or 'the strong God.' This term emphasizes God's power and authority in Abram's calling. In this verse, it reminds us that it is God who directs and guides our steps, calling us to trust Him. Spiritually, it encourages us to recognize God's sovereignty in our lives, even when we face the unknown.

The name 'Haran' designates an important city in Abram's narrative. It represents a place of stagnation, where Abram and his family stayed before responding to God's call. The city sometimes symbolizes the places of comfort that hold us back, while God calls us to move forward. It teaches us that to follow God, we may need to leave our comfort zones and attachments.

4.epoque: This passage is set in an ancient context, around 2000 B.C., at a time when nomadic families moved according to resources and divine promises.
4.passage: In this chapter, God calls Abram to leave his homeland for a promised land, marking the beginning of a new era in the plan of salvation. This departure is an act of faith that establishes Abram as a model of trust in God.
4.culture: At that time, family relationships and territorial attachments were paramount. Leaving one's family and country was an act of great faith and sacrifice, often perceived as risky.
4.interpretation: This verse illustrates Abram's response to the divine call, emphasizing the importance of obedience and faith. It reminds us that God calls each of us to step out of our comfort zones to follow Him, even when we do not know the way.
4.commentaire: Abram's departure is a powerful example of faith in action. At 75 years old, he demonstrates that age is not an obstacle to responding to God's call. This passage encourages us to be attentive to God's instructions and to be ready to act, even when it involves personal sacrifices.

mots.sens: The name 'Abram' means 'exalted father' and is derived from the Hebrew root 'רם' (ram), which means 'to elevate.' This name carries a divine promise, as God will transform Abram into 'Abraham,' the father of a multitude. It underscores Abram's unique calling in God's plan of salvation, where he becomes the patriarch of Israel and a model of faith.

The name 'Saraï' means 'my princess' and is related to the root 'שר' (sar), which means 'prince' or 'leader.' This name reflects Saraï's special status in the divine plan, as she will be the mother of Isaac, the heir of the promises made to Abram. The transformation of Saraï into 'Sarah' also highlights her crucial role in the fulfillment of God's promises.

The word 'Charan' designates a city in Mesopotamia, which was an important commercial and cultural center. This place is significant because it is where Abram received God's call to leave his homeland. Charan represents a transitional stage, where Abram is prepared to enter the promised land, emphasizing the importance of obedience in the journey of faith.

The term 'Canaan' designates the land promised by God to Abram and his descendants. It is often associated with the idea of blessing and divine inheritance. Canaan also symbolizes the place where God will establish His people, indicating that the land is not only geographical but also spiritual, representing the promise of communion with God.

5.epoque: The account of Abram is set in the ancient context of the Middle East, around the second millennium B.C., a time marked by tribal migrations and complex relationships between peoples.
5.passage: This passage occurs at the beginning of Abram's call, in chapter 12 of Genesis, marking a turning point in biblical history, where God begins to establish a people for Himself through Abram.
5.culture: In the culture of the time, travel was often associated with challenges and uncertainties, but also with divine promises. Movements were often motivated by economic or spiritual reasons.
5.interpretation: This verse illustrates Abram's obedience to God's call, highlighting his faith and willingness to leave what is familiar to follow divine direction. It reminds us of the importance of faith in our own walk with God.
5.commentaire: Abram's departure to Canaan is a model of faith and obedience for today's believers. Like Abram, we are called to leave our comfort zones to follow God's will. This passage encourages us to trust in God's promises, even when the path seems uncertain.

mots.sens: This term means 'land' or 'country' and is often used in the Bible to designate specific territories or the promised land. In this context, it emphasizes the importance of the land that God has promised to Abram and his descendants. Spiritually, it evokes the idea of divine inheritance and God's promise to establish a people on this land.

Sichem is a historical city mentioned in the Bible, often associated with significant events in Israel's history. It represents a place of encounter and divine revelation, where God promised the land to Abram. Theologically, Sichem symbolizes the beginning of the possession of the promised land and Israel's commitment to God.

Moré means 'teacher' or 'one who teaches,' and in this context, it refers to a place where Abram encountered sacred oaks. This can symbolize wisdom and divine revelation, suggesting that God teaches Abram His will. Spiritually, it indicates the importance of listening to God's voice in places of encounter.

This term designates the Canaanites, the people who inhabited the promised land before the arrival of the Israelites. The Canaanites often represent opposition to God's will and the challenges that the people of Israel will have to overcome. It highlights the struggle between God's people and the forces that oppose His plan.

6.epoque: This passage is set in the patriarchal era, when God calls Abram to leave his homeland to enter into a new promise. It is a pivotal moment in Israel's history, marking the beginning of the covenant between God and Abram.
6.passage: In this chapter, God calls Abram to leave his country and family to go to a land that He will show him. This journey is the beginning of a new life for Abram, where he will be the father of a great nation.
6.culture: At that time, land was perceived as a divine gift and a symbol of blessing. The oaks of Moré, often associated with places of worship, indicate that the encounter with God takes place in natural and sacred spaces.
6.interpretation: This verse highlights Abram's faith, who, despite the presence of the Canaanites, chooses to follow God's call. It reminds us that faith can lead us through unknown territories, even in the face of opposition or challenges.
6.commentaire: Abram's journey to Sichem is a powerful example of faith and obedience to God's call. As believers, we are also called to leave our comfort zones to follow the direction God gives us. This passage encourages us to trust God, even when we face obstacles, knowing that He has a plan for our lives.

mots.sens: The name 'Abram' means 'exalted father' and is derived from the Hebrew root 'אַב', which means 'father'. This name emphasizes the divine promise to make Abram the father of a great nation, which is central to God's plan for humanity. Spiritually, it evokes faith and obedience, as Abram responds to God's call with trust.

The term 'erets' means 'land' or 'country'. In this context, it refers to the land promised by God to Abram and his descendants. This word is filled with promise and destiny, symbolizing not only a geographical location but also a spiritual inheritance for God's people.

The word 'mizbeach' means 'altar'. It is used to designate a place of worship and sacrifice, where homage is paid to God. The construction of an altar by Abram indicates his recognition of the divine presence and his commitment to authentic worship, highlighting the importance of adoration in the relationship with God.

The verb 'nira' means 'to appear' or 'to manifest'. In this verse, it emphasizes God's initiative to reveal Himself to Abram, marking a crucial moment in the history of redemption. This appearance is an invitation to communion and divine revelation, essential for faith.

7.epoque: This passage is set in an ancient context, around the middle of the second millennium B.C., at a time when the patriarchs played a central role in the history of Israel.
7.passage: In this chapter, God calls Abram to leave his homeland for a land that He promises him. This moment is crucial as it marks the beginning of the covenant between God and Abram, and by extension, with his people.
7.culture: At this time, the construction of altars was a common practice to honor the gods and establish places of worship. This reflects the religious culture of the ancients, where sacrifices were a means to draw closer to the divine.
7.interpretation: This verse illustrates God's faithfulness to His promises and the importance of Abram's faith. By building an altar, Abram acknowledges God's presence and commits to obeying Him, which serves as a model for all believers.
7.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God reveals Himself to those who are willing to follow Him. Abram's response, through the construction of an altar, teaches us the importance of worship and recognizing divine sovereignty in our lives. As Christians, we are called to build 'altars' in our hearts, testifying to our commitment to God and our gratitude for His promises.

mots.sens: This word means 'tent' and refers to a temporary shelter, often used by nomads. It evokes the idea of mobility and dependence on God for provision. In the context of Abraham's faith, it symbolizes his detachment from material possessions and his commitment to follow divine direction.

This term designates an 'altar', a place of sacrifice and devotion to God. It is often associated with worship and communion with the Lord. In this verse, the construction of an altar by Abraham underscores the importance of praise and recognition of God's presence in his life.

This verb means 'to invoke' or 'to call'. It implies an action of prayer or supplication, marking a personal relationship with God. In this passage, it shows that Abraham does not settle for a ritual act but seeks a living interaction with the Eternal.

The name 'Bethel' means 'house of God'. It is a symbolic place where Abraham establishes a strong spiritual connection. It reminds believers that every place where they meet God becomes a sacred space, conducive to divine encounter.

8.epoque: This passage is set in the patriarchal context, around the second millennium B.C., a time marked by tribal movements and the establishment of divine promises to Abraham and his descendants.
8.passage: In this chapter, Abraham, having received God's call, begins his journey of faith. Verse 8 illustrates his obedience and devotion by pitching tents and building an altar, symbols of his relationship with God.
8.culture: At this time, altars were places of sacrifice and worship, essential in nomadic culture. They served to establish points of encounter with the divine and affirm the faith of the ancestors.
8.interpretation: The fact that Abraham invokes the name of the Lord after building an altar shows the importance of worship in the life of faith. It also emphasizes that faith is manifested through concrete actions and moments of communion with God.
8.commentaire: This verse teaches us that our relationship with God must be nourished by moments of worship and prayer. Like Abraham, we are called to build 'altars' in our lives, places where we can meet with God and entrust our lives to Him. It also reminds us of the importance of remaining mobile in our faith, ready to follow the direction that God indicates.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to walk' or 'to go'. It evokes not only physical movement but also a spiritual journey. In the context of Abram, it underscores his obedience to the divine call and his progression in faith. Abram's journey south also symbolizes a journey of discovery and dependence on God.

This word designates the direction 'south'. In biblical culture, the south is often associated with warmth, prosperity, and fertile lands. Spiritually, heading south can symbolize a search for blessings and divine promises, such as those God made to Abram.

9.epoque: This passage is set in antiquity, at a time when the patriarchs were establishing relationships with God and covenants that would shape the history of Israel.
9.passage: In Genesis 12, God calls Abram to leave his homeland for a promised land. This verse marks the continuity of his journey of faith, illustrating his obedience and trust in God.
9.culture: At this time, travels were often long and perilous, and the direction south could involve challenges but also opportunities for growth and prosperity.
9.interpretation: Abram moves south, symbolizing his progression in faith and his commitment to follow divine direction. This teaches us the importance of walking according to God's will, even when the path seems uncertain.
9.commentaire: This verse reminds us that walking with God is a continuous process that requires faith and obedience. Like Abram, we are called to move toward God's promises, trusting in His guidance. Every step we take in our spiritual lives brings us closer to our divine destination.

mots.sens: This word means 'famine' and evokes a period of severe food shortage. It is derived from the root meaning 'to be hungry' and emphasizes the anguish and desperate need that famine brings. Spiritually, famine can symbolize a lack of spiritual resources or the presence of God in an individual's life.

This term refers to Egypt, a country often associated with oppression and idolatry in the Bible. The root of the word evokes notions of 'limit' or 'restriction,' which can symbolize the spiritual constraints encountered when straying from the promised land. In this context, Egypt represents a temporary refuge but also a place of spiritual danger.

This verb means 'to descend' and can be interpreted both physically and spiritually. In the biblical narrative, descending to Egypt often implies a movement toward a place of danger or away from God. Spiritually, this can symbolize a choice to turn away from divine promise to seek human solutions.

10.epoque: The narrative takes place in a patriarchal context, as Abram (later Abraham) is receiving God's promises regarding his descendants and the land that will be given to him.
10.passage: This verse is found in the chapter where God calls Abram to leave his homeland and go to a land that God will show him. The famine that arises tests Abram's faith and pushes him to make crucial decisions.
10.culture: In antiquity, famines were devastating events that could force families and individuals to migrate to more prosperous regions, often to Egypt, which was known for its agricultural wealth.
10.interpretation: Spiritually, Abram's choice to descend into Egypt can be seen as a lack of trust in God in the face of adversity. It reminds us that even in times of crisis, we must seek divine direction rather than rely on our own solutions.
10.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of remaining faithful to God's direction, even when circumstances seem desperate. Abram's descent into Egypt warns us against the risk of seeking refuge in places or solutions that may lead us away from our divine calling. In times of spiritual or material famine, let us turn to God for the wisdom and provision we need.

mots.sens: This term means 'woman' or 'wife.' It is derived from the Hebrew root that evokes the idea of relationship and closeness. In the context of this verse, it highlights the intimate bond between Abram and Sarai, illuminating the beauty not only of their physical union but also of their spiritual connection. The mention of 'woman' here is also significant, as it establishes Sarai's role in God's divine plan for Abram's descendants.

This word means 'beautiful' or 'pretty.' It is often used in Hebrew literature to describe not only physical appearance but also the splendor and allure that can inspire admiration. In this verse, it emphasizes Sarai's beauty, which is recognized even in a foreign land, and can be interpreted as a reflection of God's goodness in creation.

This word refers to Egypt, a country often symbolic in the Bible, representing oppression and idolatry. In Abram's narrative, Egypt is a place of temporary refuge, but also a location where spiritual and moral challenges may arise. The mention of Egypt here underscores the contrast between God's promise for the land of Canaan and the potential dangers of life in a foreign country.

11.epoque: This passage is set in a patriarchal context, around 2000 B.C., at a time when alliances and interpersonal relationships were often determined by social and political considerations.
11.passage: In this chapter, Abram, obeying God's call, leaves his homeland for a promised land. Before entering Egypt, he expresses his fears regarding the beauty of his wife and the potential dangers she might encounter.
11.culture: In the culture of the time, physical beauty could attract attention but also provoke desires. Arranged marriages and alliances were common, and a woman's beauty could influence the decisions of powerful men.
11.interpretation: This verse highlights human vulnerability in the face of fear and danger. Abram, though a man of faith, shows concern that leads him to manipulate the truth to protect his wife, thus underscoring the tension between faith and fear in the lives of believers.
11.commentaire: This passage reminds us that even men of faith can face moments of doubt and fear. It encourages us to trust God in difficult situations rather than resorting to human schemes. Sarai's beauty is a reminder that God creates and calls each person to a purpose, and that our worth does not depend on the opinions of others, but on our identity in Christ.

mots.sens: This word means 'woman' or 'wife.' In the Hebrew context, it refers to the marital relationship and the protection that a man should offer his wife. Spiritually, this underscores the importance of unity and trust in marriage, as well as the vulnerability of women in patriarchal societies.

This term means 'to die' or 'to be killed.' It evokes the gravity of the threat that Abraham feels for his life. Theologically, it reminds us of the reality of danger and fear that believers may encounter, but also the necessity of faith in God for protection.

This word refers to 'Egyptian' and relates to the inhabitants of ancient Egypt. In the biblical narrative, Egyptians are often associated with oppression and idolatry. This highlights the contrast between God's people and the surrounding nations, as well as the challenges believers face in hostile contexts.

12.epoque: This passage is set in a patriarchal context of antiquity, where travel and interactions between different nations were often marked by tensions and conflicts.
12.passage: In this chapter, God calls Abraham to leave his homeland to enter into a divine promise. This verse illustrates Abraham's fear in the face of the potential threat from the Egyptians, highlighting his humanity and doubts.
12.culture: The culture of the time valued family protection and survival at all costs. Women were often perceived as valuable objects, which heightened the risk for Abraham of losing his life to protect his wife.
12.interpretation: This verse highlights Abraham's fear of the unknown and his instinct to protect Sarai. Spiritually, it reminds us that even men of faith can experience doubts and fears, but that God is always present to guide them.
12.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of trusting God even in difficult situations. Abraham, though a man of faith, shows that fear can sometimes cloud our judgment. As believers, we must learn to place our worries in God's hands, knowing that He is our protector and guide in times of uncertainty.

mots.sens: This word means 'my sister' and comes from the root 'אח' (ach), which denotes a relationship of brotherhood or closeness. In this context, it emphasizes the familial connection between Abram and Sarai, while revealing Abram's manipulation for his own safety. Spiritually, this reminds us that even the patriarchs sometimes acted out of fear rather than faith.

This term means 'good' or 'well' and is often used in the Bible to denote what is pleasant or beneficial. In this verse, it reflects Abram's desire to be treated favorably, thus highlighting human concern for material well-being. Theologically, this challenges us on how we seek the favor of others instead of fully relying on God.

This word means 'soul' or 'life', and it is often associated with the idea of vitality and the essence of a person. In this passage, Abram expresses his desire to live through Sarai, revealing a human dependence rather than trust in God. This reminds us of the importance of our soul and our relationship with God for our true life.

13.epoque: This passage is set in the ancient context of the patriarchate, where travel was often dangerous and survival depended on the protection of loved ones.
13.passage: In Genesis 12, Abram receives God's call to leave his homeland, but he faces challenges in Egypt, prompting him to make decisions based on fear.
13.culture: In antiquity, family alliances and blood relations were crucial, and women were often seen as valuable objects that could influence the treatment of men.
13.interpretation: Abram, by asking Sarai to present herself as his sister, shows a human weakness in the face of fear. This illustrates the tendency to resort to schemes instead of trusting God for protection.
13.commentaire: This verse teaches us the importance of faith in God, even in difficult situations. Instead of seeking human solutions, we must remember that our security and well-being come from our relationship with Him. This encourages us to be honest and to trust God in all our circumstances.

mots.sens: This word means 'woman' and is often used in the context of marital relationships. It evokes not only the female gender but also the role and dignity of women in society. In this verse, it highlights the beauty of Abram and Sarai, and their importance in the divine plan, as their descendants will be blessed.

This term means 'beautiful' or 'pretty' and is used to describe an outward beauty that attracts attention. In biblical culture, physical beauty can have social and spiritual implications, such as being favored or attracting blessings. Here, it highlights God's providence in Abram's life, using Sarai's beauty to fulfill His purposes.

This word designates Egypt, a symbolic country in the Bible, often associated with oppression and idolatry. Egypt also represents a temporary refuge for those fleeing famine or persecution. In this context, it serves as a backdrop for the interaction between Abram's faith and the challenges he faces.

14.epoque: This passage is set in antiquity, at a time when travel was often motivated by survival, such as famine, and where relationships between peoples were marked by alliances and conflicts.
14.passage: In this chapter, Abram, obeying God's call, leaves his homeland to go to Canaan. However, faced with a famine, he goes to Egypt, raising questions about his faith and dependence on God.
14.culture: In Egyptian culture, beauty was highly valued and could influence political and social relationships. Sarai's beauty attracts the attention of the Egyptians, which has consequences for Abram's life.
14.interpretation: This verse highlights Sarai's beauty, which attracts the Egyptians, shedding light on the challenges Abram faces as a foreigner. It reminds us that even in difficult situations, God's providence is at work, and our trust in Him should prevail over our fears.
14.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of faith and trust in God, even when circumstances seem threatening. Abram, although a man of faith, faces doubts and fears. This reminds us that our inner beauty, nourished by our relationship with God, is what should guide us in times of uncertainty.

mots.sens: This word means 'woman' or 'wife'. It is derived from the Hebrew root that evokes the notion of closeness and relationship. In this verse, it emphasizes not only the physical beauty of Sarai but also her importance as Abraham's partner in faith. Spiritually, this reminds us that woman is a precious gift from God, having an essential place in the divine plan.

This term designates the king of Egypt, representing authority and power. It is often associated with oppression and resistance to God in the Scriptures. In this context, Pharaoh embodies the temptation of human power in the face of faith, illustrating how the world can sometimes value what is superficial at the expense of divine truth.

This word means 'house' and evokes the idea of refuge, family, and community. In the context of this verse, it highlights Sarai's transition to an environment that, although seemingly prestigious, is actually far from God's promise. Theologically, this reminds us that the choices we make can lead us away from our true spiritual home.

15.epoque: This passage is set in the ancient context of the Middle East, where dynasties and kingdoms were often competing for power and resources, and where the beauty of women was often a political issue.
15.passage: In Genesis 12, we witness the first step of Abraham's journey to the promised land. This verse illustrates the dangers and compromises that Abraham and Sarai face in Egypt, highlighting the challenges of faith in times of uncertainty.
15.culture: Egyptian culture valued beauty and status, which explains why Sarai is praised before Pharaoh. This reflects the social norms of the time, where marital alliances could strengthen political power.
15.interpretation: This verse highlights the vulnerability of believers in the face of worldly temptations. It reminds us that even men of faith can face situations where they must choose between trusting God and the seductions of earthly power.
15.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of standing firm in our faith, even when circumstances seem difficult. Like Abraham, we must be cautious and seek God's guidance in our decisions. Ultimately, our trust must be placed in Him, for He is the one who guides and protects those who rely on His promise.

mots.sens: This term refers to the notion of wealth and material blessing. In the context of Abram, it emphasizes how God can use unexpected means to bless His people, even through ambiguous situations. It reminds us that blessings can come from unexpected sources, and that God is sovereign over all things, including the circumstances of our lives.

This word means 'because of' or 'due to'. It indicates that Abram's actions had direct consequences on his material situation. This highlights the biblical principle that our choices can influence our well-being, and that God's favor can manifest even through decisions that seem compromised.

This term designates servants, often associated with wealth and social status. In the context of Abram, it shows that his prosperity is not limited to material goods, but also includes the people around him. This underscores the idea that true wealth includes relationships and responsibilities toward others.

This word means 'cattle', representing a form of wealth in ancient times. Cattle were a symbol of prosperity and divine blessing. In this verse, it reminds us that God's blessings can manifest in various forms, and that our trust in Him can lead us to unexpected abundance.

16.epoque: This passage is set in the patriarchal era, where tribal relationships and economic exchanges were essential for the survival and prosperity of families. Abram, as a patriarch, navigates a world where material wealth was often perceived as a divine blessing.
16.passage: In this chapter, Abram is in Egypt due to a famine in the land of Canaan. This moment illustrates the challenges he faces as a believer, and how God intervenes even in difficult circumstances to provide for his needs.
16.culture: In the culture of the time, wealth was often measured by the number of cattle and servants. Alliances and relationships were crucial, and material blessings were often seen as signs of divine approval.
16.interpretation: This verse shows that even in complicated situations, God can act to bless His people. Abram's prosperity, although arising from a delicate situation, underscores God's sovereignty over the events of our lives and His ability to use all things for our good.
16.commentaire: This passage reminds us that God can use even our mistakes or questionable choices to accomplish His purposes. As believers, we must remain aware that our decisions have consequences, and that God's blessing can manifest unexpectedly. This encourages us to trust in His providence, even when circumstances seem uncertain.

mots.sens: This term means 'to strike' or 'to wound'. It is often used in the context of divine judgments or punishments. In this verse, it emphasizes God's direct action against Pharaoh, indicating that the plagues are a divine response to an offense. The theological scope here is that God protects those who belong to Him, even in difficult situations.

The word designates the king of Egypt, representing earthly authority and power. Pharaoh is often associated with opposition to God and His people. In this context, he symbolizes human resistance to divine will, and his punishment underscores God's sovereignty over all nations.

This word means 'house' or 'home'. It evokes not only the physical place but also the notion of family and relationships. In the context of this verse, it indicates that the consequences of Pharaoh's sin affect not only himself but also his household, illustrating the idea that sin has repercussions on the entire community.

The name of Sarai, which means 'princess', emphasizes her status and importance in the divine plan. As Abram's wife, she is at the heart of God's promise for the descendants. God's protection of Sarai shows that divine promises are unshakeable and that God watches over those who are faithful to Him.

17.epoque: This passage is set in the context of the Old Testament, at a time when patriarchs like Abram were seeking the promised land and where relationships between peoples were often marked by conflicts and fragile alliances.
17.passage: In Genesis 12, God calls Abram to leave his homeland for a land that He will show him. This chapter highlights the beginnings of Abram's journey, his faith, and the challenges he encounters, including his stay in Egypt where he must face unforeseen consequences.
17.culture: At this time, polygamy and marital alliances were common, and a woman's beauty could attract the attention of the powerful. The protection of women in vulnerable situations was often overlooked, but here, God intervenes to defend Sarai.
17.interpretation: This verse reminds us that God is attentive to justice and that He defends those who are oppressed. The suffering of Pharaoh and his household is a demonstration of God's power and His ability to intervene in history to protect His promises.
17.commentaire: This passage teaches us that even in complicated situations, God is sovereign and watches over His children. He is a defender of those in danger, and we can trust in His protection. As believers, we are called to rely on God in times of uncertainty, knowing that He acts in our favor.

mots.sens: This Hebrew word means 'woman' and is often used in the context of marital relationships. It emphasizes the dignity and status of women in society. In this verse, the revelation of Abram's identity as Sarai's husband highlights the protection and responsibility that men must have toward their wives, a notion echoed in biblical teaching on marriage.

This term means 'what' or 'that'. It expresses a strong inquiry and emphasizes astonishment or incomprehension. In the context of Pharaoh's question, it shows his indignation at Abram's deception, highlighting the seriousness of the consequences of our actions on others.

This word means 'heavy' or 'serious', but it is also used to describe a serious situation. In this verse, it evokes the weight of the consequences that Abram's actions have had on himself and on Pharaoh. It reminds us that our choices can have significant repercussions, both on our lives and on the lives of others.

18.epoque: The narrative is set in an ancient context, during the patriarchal period, where relationships between tribes and nations were often marked by alliances and conflicts. It is a time when survival depended on interpersonal relationships and promises made.
18.passage: This passage is found in chapter 12 of Genesis, which recounts the beginnings of Abram's call by God. It highlights the challenges Abram faces as he goes to Egypt, underscoring the tensions between his faith and the realities of life.
18.culture: In the culture of the time, loyalty and protection of family were paramount. The revelation of a woman's identity could have heavy implications, both personally and socially, making Pharaoh's question all the more relevant.
18.interpretation: Spiritually, this verse underscores the importance of truth and integrity in our relationships. Abram's deception, though motivated by fear, illustrates how a lack of trust in God can lead to painful consequences and misunderstandings.
18.commentaire: This passage reminds us that truth is essential in our interactions with others. As believers, we must seek to be transparent and honest, even in difficult situations. Trust in God should guide our decisions to avoid complications that could harm our testimony and relationships.

mots.sens: This word means 'my sister.' It derives from the root 'אח' (ach), which means 'brother.' In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the familial bond and closeness between Abraham and Sarah, but also the manipulation of the truth. Spiritually, this reminds us of the importance of honesty and trust in relationships.

This term means 'woman' or 'wife.' It is derived from the root 'איש' (ish), which means 'man.' In this context, it highlights the sacred relationship of marriage between Abraham and Sarah, and underscores the seriousness of the situation when Abraham jeopardized this union. Theologically, this reminds us that marriage is a divine institution to be protected.

This verb means 'to take' or 'to receive.' It evokes the idea of acquiring or seizing something. In this verse, it is used to describe how the king took Sarah, which highlights the consequences of Abraham's deception. Spiritually, this underscores that our actions can have repercussions on others and on our relationship with God.

19.epoque: This passage is set in the patriarchal era, where God's promises to Abraham are being fulfilled, and where relationships between nations are often marked by conflict and misunderstanding.
19.passage: In this chapter, Abraham goes to Egypt due to a famine, and he fears for his life because of the beauty of his wife, Sarah. He lies by saying she is his sister, which leads to complications with Pharaoh.
19.culture: In the culture of the time, family alliances were crucial, and a woman's beauty could attract the attention of the powerful. The protection of a woman was often linked to the reputation of the man representing her.
19.interpretation: This verse illustrates the consequences of fear and deceit. Abraham, in seeking to protect his own life, endangers that of his wife, revealing the fragility of human faith in the face of adversity. Spiritually, this reminds us that God is sovereign and protects those who trust Him.
19.commentaire: This passage teaches us the importance of truth and trust in God during difficult times. Abraham, although a man of faith, faltered due to his fear. This reminds us that even believers can be tempted to resort to human means for protection, but God remains faithful and intervenes to correct our mistakes and protect His promises.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to send back' or 'to return.' It evokes the idea of restoring a previous situation, an action of returning to a state of peace or normalcy. In the context of this verse, it shows Pharaoh's decision to send Abraham and Sarah back, thus highlighting God's sovereignty over the nations and the protection of His people. Spiritually, this reminds us that God intervenes to free those who are in distress.

This term means 'woman' or 'wife.' It is used to designate a partner in marriage, symbolizing unity and complementarity. In this passage, it emphasizes the importance of the relationship between Abraham and Sarah, and how this relationship is protected by God. It also reminds us of the value God places on human relationships and family.

This word means 'what' or 'that which.' In this context, it can be interpreted as a question about the nature of Abraham's possessions. This highlights the wealth and blessings that God grants to those who are faithful to Him. Spiritually, it invites us to reflect on what we possess and how it is a gift from God.

20.epoque: This passage is set in the ancient context of the Middle East, where relationships between nations were often marked by conflict and alliances. Abraham, as a patriarch, navigates a world where faith and survival are closely intertwined.
20.passage: Genesis 12 recounts the beginning of God's call to Abraham and his migration to Canaan. This verse, in particular, highlights Pharaoh's reaction to Abraham and Sarah's situation, revealing divine protection over them.
20.culture: In the culture of the time, kings and pharaohs had immense power, and their decisions could change the fate of an individual. The fact that Pharaoh sends Abraham and Sarah back with their possessions shows a certain recognition of divine authority.
20.interpretation: This verse illustrates how God protects those who are faithful to Him, even in difficult circumstances. Pharaoh's decision to send Abraham and Sarah back demonstrates God's sovereignty over the hearts of kings and rulers.
20.commentaire: This passage teaches us that even when we face challenges, God is always at work to protect and restore us. It also reminds us of the importance of our relationships and how God watches over our lives. As believers, we can trust that God will intervene for our good, just as He did for Abraham.
